title: Should Self-Help Books Belong in the ELA Classroom?
author: Matt Hutson
summary: Matt Hutson argues that self-help and professional-development books deserve a place alongside literature in English Language Arts classrooms—not because they carry the same literary value, but because they give students practice evaluating the practical advice that will inevitably try to shape them as adults. The article distinguishes two traditions of serious reading: literature, which asks readers to interpret human experience through story, ambiguity, and consequence; and practical nonfiction, which makes explicit claims about how to learn, communicate, decide, and act. Hutson contends that ELA's stated purposes—identifying claims, evaluating evidence, analyzing rhetoric, comparing viewpoints, communicating clearly—already cover precisely what students need to assess a self-help argument, and that the genre's notorious weaknesses (overconfident claims, survivorship bias, correlation-causation confusion) make it ideal material for developing critical judgment rather than a reason for exclusion. He proposes an Advice Laboratory framing in which students trace the full arc of a claim—problem definition, explanatory model, specific recommendation, and testable result—and run modest low-risk experiments to move from passive consumption toward critical, experiential literacy. The piece also argues that practical knowledge functions as social capital: students with professional-network access absorb it from family; students without it often receive nothing, and a thoughtfully designed ELA curriculum could help make visible the interpretive frameworks that currently arrive unevenly by birthright. Hutson is careful to note that literature should remain central—it restores the human complexity that self-help simplifies—but argues students should graduate knowing how to read advice skeptically, not just stories deeply.
points: ELA's formal purposes—identifying claims, evaluating evidence, analyzing rhetoric, comparing viewpoints—are precisely the skills needed to assess a self-help argument, suggesting the genre belongs in ELA not despite its weaknesses but because of them; the genre's overconfident claims, correlation-causation errors, and survivorship bias are ideal material for developing critical judgment.

The Advice Laboratory framing reframes a self-help text as a claim to investigate rather than scripture or rubbish: students trace problem definition, explanatory model, specific recommendation, and testable result, then run a modest experiment to move from passive reading toward critical, experiential literacy.

Practical knowledge functions as social capital—students from professional-network families absorb models for interpreting career, money, and workplace situations by osmosis, while students without that access often receive nothing; a well-designed ELA curriculum could partially equalize access to interpretive frameworks currently distributed unevenly by birthright.

Literature should remain central precisely because it restores what practical books remove: the human complexity, ambiguity, and consequence that a model of habits or communication necessarily simplifies out, making the best curriculum pair a novel's resistance to pat answers with a practical text's explicit recommendations.

The key safeguard is treating practical texts as arguments, not authorities: students must be able to accept, reject, adapt, or further investigate the advice, and teachers must ensure a range of cultural perspectives on success, rest, ethics, and community appear alongside books fixated on individual achievement.
quotes: Most of the books I studied in English class told stories about people trying to live. Many of the books I began reading later tried to tell me how to live.
A novel can remain unresolved in the mind for years. It can grow alongside us, revealing something different each time we return to it.

A self-help or professional-development book is, among other things, an argument. The author identifies a problem, proposes an explanation, and recommends a response. The book may use data, expert testimony, personal stories, historical examples, analogies, case studies, emotional appeals, or some unstable mixture of all six.
Students will encounter these claims whether schools prepare them or not. The question is whether they will learn to treat advice as something to be examined, or merely as something to accept,

Perhaps students should learn to read stories deeply and advice skeptically. They should be able to appreciate language, follow an argument, question an author, test a claim, revise their judgment, and decide what deserves to become part of their lives.
Maybe the better question is whether students should graduate knowing how to evaluate the advice that will inevitably try to shape them.
What might change if students left English class able not only to identify a theme, but also to examine a piece of advice before allowing it to become one of the themes of their lives?
